_comment: Listings a human or Claude has read in full and cleared, with the reason. The detector is high-recall and will keep flagging these on every run, so record the screening decision here rather than loosening the regexes and losing real hits elsewhere. Keyed by file path.
content/destinations/clinics/vaia-beauty: First person restored deliberately. Vaia Pappas is a herbalist and skin therapist, not a registered health practitioner, and the venue offers no injectables, laser or needling, so AHPRA s133 does not reach it. The narrated treatment is a facial and a massage, which are cosmetic services the Code does not restrict. The LED, the infrared sauna and the hand-mixed herbal formulas are named on the menu in third person with no personal-use claim and no efficacy claim attached to any of them.
content/destinations/clinics/the-victori: Claim hit is 'prevention rather than cure' inside Derya Koch's quote describing her general approach. It is a statement of clinical philosophy, not a claim that any named treatment prevents or cures a disease, and no product or service is attached to it.
content/destinations/spas-retreats/five-: First person restored. The narrated treatment is an Ultraceuticals facial with the machinery declined, which is cosmetic. Removed: sonophoresis described as '1000x more effective than straight massage', an unsubstantiated quantitative claim. Owner quotes about her own career history are not testimonials.
content/destinations/travel/three-days-i: Detector hits are metaphorical: 'stay laser-focused on your craft'. The dermatologist content concerns Dr Lancer's skincare method, which is cosmetic rather than a therapeutic good, so the practitioner-endorsement rule does not reach it. A travel guide, not a clinic listing.
content/destinations/spas-retreats/sydne: Only device hit is an infrared sauna named as a hotel spa facility, with no efficacy claim attached to it. Not a regulated health service. The piece also discloses in its own text that Sig is the spa's Ambassador, which is the correct treatment for an endorsement, since disclosure cures endorsements even though it never cures testimonials.
content/destinations/spas-retreats/chate: Infrared sauna named as one facility in a Hydro Lounge, no claim attached. Hotel spa, no regulated health service.
content/destinations/travel/go-tos-natur: Infrared sauna named among the bathhouse circuit (steam room, Finnish sauna, ice bath) with no claim about what any of it does. Bathhouse, not a clinic.
content/destinations/travel/mondrian-gol: 'Hydrogen water, LED beds and zero-gravity naps' listed as hotel spa facilities, no efficacy claim attached to any of them.
content/destinations/travel/1-hotel-melb: First-person hit is 'Checking in, I noticed the staff first', ordinary travel writing unconnected to any device. Red light and infrared PEMF are now named as spa facilities with the sleep, recovery and nervous-system indications removed. A hotel review, not a clinic listing.
content/destinations/clinics/karpatimedi: First person restored. The narrated treatment is Eva Karpati's gentle facial with no machines used, which is cosmetic; laser and IPL appear on the menu and as the business the Karpatis distribute, never as something had. Removed: named clients credited with 'perfect pores', a relayed account of the Geneo+ from third parties, and speculation about what the machines would have achieved. Remaining claim hits are an interior-design caption about eliminating coldness, and the string 'treats' inside 'techno-treats'.
content/destinations/salons/amy-jean-eye: First person restored. The narrated treatment is a brow shape and a lash lift, both cosmetic; laser and LED appear on the service menu only and were not had. Refiled to salons/. 'The best at her business' is puffery about brow artistry, not a superiority claim about a regulated health service.
content/destinations/bathhouses/merse-we: 'You will leave loose' describes a bathhouse and sauna circuit. No regulated health service, no therapeutic good, and no claim about treating anything.
content/destinations/wellness/reju-bradd: 'Leave you feeling grounded rather than clinical' describes the timber interior of the rooms, not a treatment outcome.
content/destinations/clinics/skyn-perth/: 'The client list has barely turned over' is a statement about client retention over twenty years, not celebrity patronage offered as evidence. No client is named or characterised.
content/destinations/clinics/wildlife-or: First person restored. The narrated treatment is a hair colour and a blow-dry, which is neither a regulated health service nor a therapeutic good. Injectables appear once, as a service available from a visiting cosmetic doctor, with no personal-use claim and no outcome claim attached. The purified-water claim has been reduced to a statement about process.
content/destinations/clinics/paddington-: First person restored. The narrated treatment is a La Prairie facial and a manicure at a beauty salon; IPL appears on the menu only. The undated 20% reader discount and the neighbouring salon's blow-dry price are removed as unverifiable, which is a consumer-law point rather than a Code one.
content/destinations/clinics/the-girl-yo: First person restored in full; no body edit was required. The narrated treatment is a Hydropeptide facial at a one-room salon, which is cosmetic. Skin needling and peels appear in the menu paragraph only, with no personal-use claim and no outcome claim attached. Refiled to clinics/ at Sig's direction.
content/destinations/clinics/me-skin-and: First person restored. The narrated treatment is the Synergie Skindulgence facial and a buccal massage, both cosmetic. Laser, mesotherapy and microneedling appear only as things to try next time, now named without indications. Removed: a celebrity's patronage used to promote a clinic that also offers laser.
content/destinations/clinics/blanc-wa/bl: First person restored. The narrated treatment is Blanc's Signature Facial, which is cosmetic, so the pre-wedding context and the result stay. The LED coda is cut rather than switched to third person, and LED is still named in the treatment list. Injectables, laser and the Plasma Pen appear on the menu with no outcome claim.
content/destinations/clinics/the-sleek-s: First person restored for the Dermasweep, the extractions and the photographs, all cosmetic. Cut: the twenty minutes under the yellow LED and the wound-healing claim, clients' before-and-after photographs on the walls, and a closing 'the aesthetic destination in Melbourne'. Marnie's practice of asking first and staying in the room is kept as a fact about her, not as a personal LED account.
content/destinations/clinics/youth-lab-c: First person restored for the Signature Facial and the Beauty Chef water. The Healite II section is cut entirely rather than rewritten, and Healite is still named in the FAQs. The Hydrafacial endorsement that doubled as an SEO link is gone; the bridal guide is linked as an Ed's note.
content/destinations/clinics/youth-lab-j: First person restored for the Advanced Facial, the Gurtler interior and the bouclé chair. Cut: the LED beat with its collagen and healing claims, and a closing verdict on the writer's skin. The Lutronic Healite is still named in the FAQs.
content/destinations/clinics/reve-skin-b: First person restored for the lash lift, the Hydrafacial and the manicure. A Hydrafacial is a facial rather than a therapeutic device, so a personal account of one is not a testimonial about a therapeutic good. Cut: the client relayed in the doorway as 'the ultimate endorsement', and two outcome claims.
